cards.headline: Nothing to discount.
cards.body: A stock can be valued from the cash a business will earn. A crypto asset earns nothing, so there is no stream of profits to discount. That leaves supply and demand doing almost all of the work in setting the price.

art.alt: One small coin with a tall price banner is dwarfed by a vast mound of many tiny coins — a single coin price versus the true size of all coins together.

cards.headline: Market cap is price times supply.
cards.body: The size of a coin is not its unit price — it is price multiplied by how many coins exist. A coin at **$2** with **100 million** in circulation has a market cap of **$200 million**. That total is what you compare.

cards.prompt: Coin A costs $0.01 and Coin B costs $50. Which one is the bigger asset?

options.label: Coin B — it costs far more

cards.explanation: Unit price alone says nothing. Coin A at $0.01 with 10 billion coins is a **$100 million** asset; Coin B at $50 with 1 million coins is only **$50 million**. Size is price times supply, every time.

cards.title: Cheap price, bigger asset
cards.caption: Coin A looks cheap at a cent and Coin B dear at fifty dollars, yet A is the larger asset. Supply, not sticker price, sets the size.

cards.headline: A low price is not 'cheap'.
cards.body: Beginners buy a coin priced in fractions of a cent because it 'could reach a dollar'. But the supply is usually gigantic, so a dollar would imply a market cap larger than the biggest companies on earth. Do the multiplication first.

cards.headline: Watch the coins not yet released.
cards.body: Circulating supply exists today. Max supply is everything that will ever exist. Price times max supply is the **fully-diluted valuation**. A coin at $2, 100 million out but 1 billion planned, has a $200 million cap — and a **$2 billion** fully-diluted value.

cards.title: The unreleased overhang
cards.caption: Only a tenth of the supply is live. The other 900 million coins are an overhang: as they release, they can weigh on the price unless demand grows to match.

cards.body: To compare two coins fairly you multiply price by supply to get the [[1]], because unit price alone hides how many coins exist.
cards.explanation: Market cap is price times circulating supply — the real size of the asset. Two coins with wildly different unit prices can be the same size, or the cheaper-looking one can be far bigger.

cards.summary: A coin's size is price times supply, not its unit price — and unreleased coins can dilute it further.
bullets: A low unit price can still mean a huge asset.
Fully-diluted value counts coins not yet released.

cards.insight: The price tag on one coin tells you almost nothing. Multiply it by the supply, and the real size finally shows up.
